title: Class 11 Chemistry — Chemistry of Non-metals Study Guide
notes: Hydrogen isotopes are protium (¹H), deuterium (²H) and tritium (³H); heavy water is D₂O. Nascent hydrogen is a traditional term for freshly generated reactive hydrogen, not a distinct stable allotrope. Hydrogen peroxide decomposes as 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ and may act as oxidant or reductant depending on its partner. Oxides may be acidic, basic, amphoteric, neutral, peroxide or mixed; classify by behavior.

Ozone is bent O₃ formed from oxygen under energetic conditions. It is a strong oxidant and absorbs UV in the stratosphere. Ozone depletion is driven especially by catalytic chlorine/bromine radicals released from long-lived compounds; reducing ozone-depleting emissions supports recovery. Ozone depletion is not the same phenomenon as climate change.

N₂ is relatively inert because its N≡N bond is strong. Ammonia is trigonal pyramidal and a weak base: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. It forms ammonium salts with acids and reacts with oxygen under suitable conditions. Concentrated ammonia is hazardous. Nitric acid is a strong acid and oxidizer; products from metals depend on concentration and conditions. Nitrate can be tested by the brown-ring test using Fe²⁺ in acid.

Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂ are diatomic oxidizing non-metals; oxidizing strength generally decreases down the group. Reactions with water, alkalis and ammonia depend on conditions. Chlorine bleaches moist material through oxidation. Hydrogen-halide acidity in water generally increases down the group (HF is weak because of strong H–F bonding), while reducing strength rises down the group.

Carbon allotropes include diamond, graphite, fullerenes and amorphous forms. CO is a colourless, highly toxic reducing gas. PH₃ (phosphine) is toxic, weakly basic and reducing. H₂S is a toxic weak acid and reducing analytical reagent. SO₂ is an acidic oxide that can act as oxidant or reductant and as a bleaching agent. H₂SO₄ is acidic and, when concentrated, oxidizing and strongly dehydrating. Sodium thiosulfate is Na₂S₂O₃ and is used in photography and iodometric titration.

Never prepare or smell toxic gases as a home experiment. For each compound organize answers as preparation, observation, chemical explanation, balanced equation and use; state conditions. Concentrated acids and reagents require trained laboratory controls.
formulas: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HOCl (simplified aqueous equilibrium)
keyPoints: Reaction products and oxidizing behavior depend on conditions, including concentration and temperature.
Halogen oxidizing strength generally decreases down the group; hydrogen-halide reducing strength generally increases.
Ozone depletion involves catalytic radical chemistry in the stratosphere.
CO, NH₃, PH₃ and H₂S present serious inhalation hazards; H₂SO₄ is corrosive.
Learn each named substance's preparation, properties, tests and uses within the prescribed syllabus.
practiceQuestions: Classify acidic, basic, amphoteric and neutral oxides and give one example of each.
Explain nitrogen's relative inertness and one cause of ozone depletion.
Compare chlorine, bromine and iodine in oxidizing strength and describe a distinguishing test observation.
State two contrasting chemical roles of SO₂ and explain why CO is hazardous.
Describe the brown-ring test for nitrate and name the reagent responsible for the coloured complex.
summary: Organize non-metal chemistry by group and compound: preparation, condition-dependent reactions, characteristic tests and uses, with appropriate safety and environmental context.
